newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - New look to bring Romania more foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New look to bring Romania more foreign investment.

text.p: Romania's new image after reformists ousted former communists from government could draw in the foreign investment it needs if the new authorities send out the right signals quickly.

Economists say President Emil Constantinescu and centrists elected to parliament had to create the right conditions to make Romania an investment haven and boost levels far below those of other ex-communist states in the region.

In a country located strategically in central Europe and blessed with resources and inexpensive skilled labour, that means speeding up selloffs of state property, lowering taxes and liberalising foreign exchanges.
"It's a total change of image now and Romania should work to preserve that image for foreign investors," said economist Teodor Nicolaescu.
Constantinescu, who defeated Ion Iliescu, Romania's leader since 1989, promised during his campaign to smash barriers to investment and bring in the new technology needed by industry.
Total direct foreign investment in the seven years since Romania's bloody upheaval ousted dictator Nicolae Ceausescu was $2.09 billion at end-October.
WHAT IS NEEDED

Most analysts blame bureaucracy and corruption, inadequate tax and accounting rules, low levels of foreign ownership of land and slow privatisation in Eastern Europe's second largest market after Poland.

"Foreign investment will rise significantly only when Romania is ready to sell something of substance, public utilities included," said Florin Bonciu, general manager of the Romanian Development Agency (ARD).
"The bulk of foreign investment in Poland or Hungary, for instance, is the result of privatisation. Hungary last year sold part of its telecommunications network."
He said Romania had also had signals from foreigners about its telecommunications but no decision was taken.
Octav Buruiana, president of the National Investors' Association, pointed to a 38 percent profit tax which he said was "no incentive".
Foreign currency markets are also a brake. The leu currency has been artificially propped on interbank markets for months about 40 percent higher than its street rate of about 4,500 to the dollar.

The new cabinet, to be made up of Constantinescu's Democratic Convention and Social Democrats (USD), is perceived by business as more committed to market reforms. Liberals accused the outgoing leftist government of stalling reforms.
"The State Ownership Fund (FPS) should be encouraged to step up sales under the mass selloff. This will bring in foreign investors," said a western analyst.
"Romania will have difficulty selling over-sized units nobody wants, but not everything is junk. It does have some highly attractive assets to sell."

A mass privatisation launched last October offered Romanians stakes of up to 60 percent in 4,000 state companies in exchange for coupons. The remaining 40 percent was left for the FPS to sell for cash to local and foreign investors.
Romania opened up to foreign investors after 1989 and a foreign investment law was passed two years later.

The law and later amendments provided incentives to foreigners, including full repatriation of profit, full retention of export earnings, tax holidays for projects of more than $50 million, and duty-free equipment imports.
But it covers only direct foreign investment, with portfolio investors having to obey its rules which sometimes mean four months of infuriating bureaucratic procedures.
"With the emergent over-the-counter (OTC) market running parallel to the bourse opening a year ago, portfolio investors should be encouraged," said a broker.
DEVELOPMENT BANK MORE OPTIMISTIC
The ARD is more optimistic about recent trends and says reported figures understate the true worth of foreign investment.
"We report paid foreign capital, rather than investment commitments," Bonciu said.

The ARD quotes the example of South Korea's Daewoo Heavy Industries Ltd, which has several projects in Romania and is its largest single investor with some $200 million despite a $1.0 billion commitment until the year 2000.
ARD officials also say land ownership is a false problem as the law allows foreigners opening Romania-based companies to buy land. "It's just a matter of how the law is applied," Bonciu said.
From last year, the ARD says, a shift was noted in foreign investors' interest towards sectors like banking and insurance, oil and gold exploration, consumer goods and services.
Last year's main projects were in detergents and brewing, from major companies including Unilever, Procter & Gambler and Brau und Brunnen.
Earlier this year, Fiat 's New Holland struck a joint venture with a local farm machinery maker, making it the third largest single investor in Romania.
"These are good signs, showing foreigners look at our country with increased interest," an ARD official said.
